content: Unilateral cerebral palsy (CP) is a neurological condition that impairs muscle control and function on one side of the body. This condition arises due to disruptions in the developing brain during the fetal or infant stages. Children with unilateral CP often struggle to use both hands together effectively, and the more affected limb is frequently neglected. Constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) is a therapeutic approach designed to enhance the use of the more affected upper limb and improve the ability to perform tasks requiring both hands. CIMT operates on two core principles: restricting the use of the less affected limb (e.g., with a splint, mitt, or sling) and engaging the more affected limb in intensive therapeutic exercises. The primary objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of CIMT in improving the function of the more affected upper limb in children with unilateral CP. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in March 2018 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PEDro, OTseeker, and others, as well as trial registries. Additional methods included citation searches, reference list reviews, expert consultations, handsearching key journals, and using Google Scholar. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cluster-RCTs, or clinically controlled trials involving children aged 0 to 19 years with unilateral CP. CIMT was compared to alternative interventions, such as different forms of CIMT, low-dose or high-dose therapies, or dose-matched upper-limb interventions like bimanual therapy. The primary outcomes assessed were bimanual performance, unimanual capacity, and manual ability. Secondary outcomes included self-care, body function, participation, and quality of life. A total of 36 trials, published between 2004 and 2018, were included, involving 1264 participants. The sample sizes ranged from 11 to 105 participants, with a mean age of 5.96 years (standard deviation 1.82), spanning from three months to 19.8 years. Of the participants, 53% were male, and 47% had left-sided hemiplegia. Across the studies, 57 different outcome measures were used. The average duration of CIMT programs was four weeks (ranging from one to 10 weeks), with session frequencies varying from twice weekly to daily. Session durations ranged from 0.5 to eight hours per day, with a mean total intervention time of 137 hours (range 20 to 504 hours). The most commonly used constraint devices were mitts/gloves or slings, each employed in 11 studies. The risk of bias across the studies was judged to be moderate to high. Key Results: 1. CIMT vs. Low-Dose Comparison (e.g., occupational therapy): CIMT demonstrated greater effectiveness than low-dose interventions in improving bimanual performance, with a mean difference (MD) of 5.44 Assisting Hand Assessment (AHA) units (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.37 to 8.51). CIMT also showed superiority in enhancing unimanual capacity, as measured by the Quality of Upper Extremity Skills Test (QUEST) across various domains: Dissociated movement: MD 5.95 (95% CI 2.02 to 9.87) Grasps: MD 7.57 (95% CI 2.10 to 13.05) Weight bearing: MD 5.92 (95% CI 2.21 to 9.60) Protective extension: MD 12.54 (95% CI 8.60 to 16.47) Adverse events were reported in three studies, including frustration, refusal to comply with the constraint, and reversible skin irritations caused by casting. 2. CIMT vs. High-Dose Comparison (e.g., individualized occupational therapy, bimanual therapy): CIMT was not more effective than high-dose interventions in improving bimanual performance (MD −0.39 AHA units, 95% CI −3.14 to 2.36). Similarly, there was no evidence of greater effectiveness for unimanual capacity in a single study using QUEST: Dissociated movement: MD 0.49 (95% CI −10.71 to 11.69) Grasp: MD −0.20 (95% CI −11.84 to 11.44) Two studies noted that some children experienced frustration during CIMT. 3. CIMT vs. Dose-Matched Comparison (e.g., Hand Arm Bimanual Intensive Therapy, bimanual therapy, occupational therapy): No significant differences were observed in bimanual performance between CIMT and dose-matched interventions (MD 0.80 AHA units, 95% CI −0.78 to 2.38). Similarly, no evidence suggested that CIMT was more effective than dose-matched interventions for unimanual capacity, as measured by: Box and Blocks Test: MD 1.11 (95% CI −0.06 to 2.28) Melbourne Assessment: MD 1.48 (95% CI −0.49 to 3.44) QUEST Dissociated movement: MD 6.51 (95% CI −0.74 to 13.76) Grasp: MD 6.63 (95% CI −2.38 to 15.65) Weight bearing: MD −2.31 (95% CI −8.02 to 3.40) An exception was noted in the Protective Extension domain, where CIMT showed a significant improvement (MD 6.86, 95% CI 0.14 to 13.58). No differences in manual ability were observed between groups (ABILHAND-Kids MD 0.74, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.18). Among 15 studies, two children were unable to tolerate CIMT, and three experienced difficulties. Conclusions: The quality of evidence across all findings was rated as low to very low. For children with unilateral CP, there is some evidence suggesting that CIMT improves bimanual performance and unimanual capacity compared to low-dose interventions. However, CIMT does not appear to offer additional benefits over high-dose or dose-matched interventions. Based on the available evidence, CIMT is considered a safe therapeutic option for children with CP.
